newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Gold - Forward sales to wane as rates rise.
newsitem.headline: Australia Gold - Forward sales to wane as rates rise.

text.p: A recent spate of producer hedging in the gold market could come to a close soon if lease rates continue to rise and gold prices continue to fall.

Australian producers, facing unfavourable currency exchange rates and higher mining costs, have been the most active hedge-takers in recent weeks in the forward markets, which has helped cause a near doubling in the one-month lease rate to around two percent, bullion dealers said.

But further declines in the U.S.-dollar-denominated gold price, and/or more strengthening in the Australian currency could make curtailing production a more attractive option than forward selling owing to borrowing costs.
In the last few days the Australian dollar has gained about a cent on the U.S. dollar while the U.S. gold price has fallen some US$5 an ounce.
"We've basically had for ourselves and for our customers twelve or thirteen dollars in Aussie (Australian) terms stripped out of the gold price," said a Sydney-based gold dealer
Gold fetches about A$441 an ounce, which is near or below the costs of many miners.
"Many producers taking out fresh forward positions have little choice and for some it's an act of desperation," said a dealer in Melbourne.
Said another dealer: "With the spot around A$440, and no contango, you either shut your mine down or you do some form of disaster forward selling."

Melbourne based consultants Surbiton Associates Pty Ltd calculates the weighted average cash cost for operations representing 82 percent of all Australian primary gold production was A$376 an ounce in the last quarter.
Using such data, and taking into account other costs, such as amortisation, depreciation and financing, there is little margin at the current price, Sandra Close of Surbiton said.
For higher cost miners, the impact can be devastating.
"There are a lot of people who will go broke in the next thirty dollars," an analyst familiar with Australia's army of "junior" miners said.
"If they haven't done something now, they are at the stage where they must," he added.
Australia miners, which in total produce about 300 tonnes of gold a year are increasingly being forced to dig deeper to maintain ore gradings, which raises costs.
